# Introduction

In this tutorial we will explore some ways to visualize RNA-seq data. Of course, there are **multiple** ways to visualize the same data, so feel free to explore different options! A great hint is to look at papers that have performed RNA-seq - see how and why they visualized their data the way they did. If you find a plot you want to reproduce, I'd be happy to help you reproduce it.

For this tutorial, we will be using the differential expression data we generated in the Tutorial 7 DESeq2 analysis worksheet. If you completed that tutorial, you'll have the DESeqDataSet object stored as a `.rds` object which we will use in this tutorial.

We will explore the following data visualization techniques:

1.  Sample Clustering Using PCA Plots
2.  Summarizing Differential Expression Data with Volcano and Bar Plots
3.  Plotting Normalized Counts
4.  Plotting Z-Score Heatmaps

**To start this tutorial, lets first load the different libraries we will need**

```{r packages, message = FALSE, warning=FALSE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(DESeq2))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(dplyr))
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(pheatmap)) # package for generating heatmaps
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Sample Clustering Using PCA Plots

After running our data through `DESeq2`, we used a PCA plot to assess the quality of our data. A PCA plot can tell us how different the overall gene expression profiles of our samples are (remember, the points that group together are more similar to each other than those that are further apart from each other). However, the default plot from DESeq2 is quite ugly... Let's try to make it better using `ggplot2`.

First, let's load our DESeq2 object (if the `dds` object is already loaded into your environment then you can skip this step). Instead of running the whole analysis again, we can just load the RDS file into our environment. RDS files allow you to store an **R object** that can then be loaded again without re-running a script. RDS objects may be very helpful for types of data that cannot be stored as a text file (*i.e.,* CSV or TSV) or data that takes a long time to process if running from scratch. We will load our RDS object with the following code:

```{r readRDS}
dds <- readRDS("data/dds.rds")
```

<br></br>

Like we did in the previous worksheet, we will log-transform our data to stabilize and normalize variance. You can also save this log-transformed R object as and RDS file!

```{r rlog}
rld <- rlog(dds)
```

<br></br>

To plot our PCA plot, we will use the following code.

We will perform our PCA analysis using the DESeq2 function, but instead of plotting it, we will specify the `returnData = TRUE` argument to return a dataframe.

```{r pca-analysis}
# Get the PCA data as a dataframe with returnData = TRUE
pcaData <- plotPCA(rld, intgroup=c("condition"), returnData = TRUE) 
glimpse(pcaData)

# Using the attr() function, we will extract the percent variation explained of each axis of the pcaData object
percentVar <- round(100 * attr(pcaData, "percentVar"))
glimpse(percentVar)
```

<br></br>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

We will use `ggplot2` to plot our data in a *pretty* way. `ggplot2` is loaded as part of the `tidyverse` package and is a nice, structured way to plot in R. `ggplot` works by plotting elements as layers. This means that different elements (like lines or points) are plotted over each other depending on what step they were added to the plot. Here is a chunk of code with some common elements to make pretty plots with `ggplot`.

```{r ggplot-example, eval = FALSE}
#example code 
data %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = variable1, y = variable2)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(), #text on the tick marks
    legend.title = element_text(), 
    panel.border = element_rect()
    ) +
  ggtitle("Plot Title") +
  xlab("x-axis label") +
  ylab("y-axis label") 
  
```

<br></br>

Here is a breakdown:

1.  `data` is the input dataframe and we can pipe it into the `ggplot()` function.
2.  We then call `ggplot`. Within `ggplot`, we've specified an `aesthetic`. When you specify things inside `aesthetic()`, it means that that element depends on the data. For the data here we want the x and y axis values to depend on variable1 and variable2 in the data, so we specify it within the `aesthetic`.
3.  We then specify a `geom` element which tells R how you want to plot your data (points, bars, lines, etc.). There are many types of geoms that you can explore!
4.  **Optional** We can specify many geoms! In this case, since `geom_line()` is plotted *after* `geom_point`, we see that the line is actually physically plotted over the points.
5.  We specify a `theme_` type. In `ggplot`, the default theme is kind of ugly, which we will see. There are many different automatic `ggplot` themes you can choose to quickly change the way your plot looks. Explore them!
6.  `theme()` is different than the `theme_` type. Within `theme()` you can change the way many elements of the plot looks. This includes, the axis text (font, colour, face), axis ticks, axis thickness, legends and legend titles, facet strips, etc. It's a very useful function!
7.  `ggtitle()` is optional. You can use it give your plot a title!
8.  `xlab()` and `ylab()`. Allows you to rename the axis titles. By default, the axis titles will be named as the variable they represent (in this case, variable1 and variable2). Alternatively, you can also use `labs(x = "xtitle", y = "ytitle")`.

**Note:** In `ggplot`, layers are added with the `+` operator, not the `%>%`!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

Now that we're a little more familiar with `ggplot` Let's start try plotting with it!

We will pipe `pcaData` into `ggplot` and since we want to plot PC1 on the x-axis and PC2 on the y-axis, we specify them in the `aesthetic`. You'll notice that since we didn't specify a `geom`, there's nothing on our plot. We never told R what we wanted to plot our data as!

```{r pca1}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2))
```

<br></br>

Next, let's add a `geom`. We want to use points to represent our samples in the PCA plot. We can use `geom_point()` to achieve this.

```{r pca2}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2)) +
  geom_point()
```

<br></br>

So far, there's a problem with this plot - we don't know which points belong to which conditions! We can colour code our points by specifying the `colour` argument in the `aesthetic`. We need to specify this inside the `aesthetic` because the colour will change **depending** on our data. If we specified colour outside of the `aesthetic`, then all the points would still be the same colour! Because we want colour to vary depending on condition, we will set `colour = condition`. The size of the points are also kind of small. We can make them bigger by specifying the `size` argument in `geom_point()`.

```{r pca3}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 4)
```

<br></br>

This is starting to look a little better. Let's resize the axis limits. We can specify the axis limits using `scale_x_continuous()` and `scale_y_continuous()`.

```{r pca4}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-10,10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-50,50)) 
```

<br></br>

Let's also modify the axis titles to reflect the percent variance we calculated in `percentVar`. We will do this using `xlab()` and `ylab()` combined with the `paste0()` function. `paste0` simply sticks multiple strings together. Since `percentVar` is a vector, we can access the values within it like so: `percentVar[1]` extracts the first value in the vector and `percentVar[2]` extracts the second value.

```{r pca5}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-10,10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-50,50)) +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ",percentVar[1],"% variance")) + 
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ",percentVar[2],"% variance")) 
```

<br></br>

Let's also change the theme! Alongside changing the theme, we can also modify some other elements. See if you can figure out how some of these elements were changed!

```{r pca6}
pcaData %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = condition)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-10,10)) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-50,50)) +
  xlab(paste0("PC1: ",percentVar[1],"% variance")) + 
  ylab(paste0("PC2: ",percentVar[2],"% variance")) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 11),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    legend.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.border = element_rect(linewidth = 2)) +
  labs(colour = "Condition")
```

That looks much better than before!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Summary of Differentially Expressed Genes

To get a broad idea of how many genes were significantly and differentially expressed in our data set we can employ two strategies:

1.  Volcano Plots
2.  Bar Plots

We will use the differential expression data from our DESeq2 analysis that has been filtered for differentially expressed genes. This data can be loaded from the `chlamy_results.csv` file that you generated as part of the previous tutorial.

```{r message = FALSE}
dat <- read_csv("data/chlamy_results.csv")
dat
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 1. Volcano Plot

A volcano plot contains the log2FoldChange of a gene on the x-axis and the -log10(p-value) on the y-axis (this transformation will make it such that the genes with **lower** p-values are showed **higher** in the y-axis).

Volcano plots are handy to visualize the distribution of genes that were highly upregulated/downregulated and whether they're significant or not.

Let's plot a volcano plot using ggplot2:

```{r}
dat %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj))) + # see that we are using the -log10() function to transform our padj values
  geom_point()
```

<br></br>

Nice, this is a start, but the plot doesn't really give us a lot of information... Let's set some boundary lines on our x and y axes to split the data into quadrants. We will do this using the `geom_hline()` and `geom_vline()` functions from ggplot2 - these functions will create a horizontal and vertical line (respectively) based on an intercept that we provide.

We will set the horizontal line at the adjusted p-value = 0.05. Since the y-axis is log-transformed, we also have to account for this! We will set two vertical lines, one at -1 and another at 1. This will help delineate genes that are differentially expressed (up or down) greater than 2X.

```{r}
dat %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj))) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed")
```

<br></br>

This is a little bit better. We can start to see that there are a huge amount of genes that were significantly upregulated/downregulated. However, it would be nice if we could add some colour to genes that are upregulated and downregulated. Unfortunately, to colour data in ggplot based on a category, you need a column that tells the program what category a row is assigned to. The good news is that we can easily label our data to do this.

To label every row in our dataset as 'upregulated' or 'downregulated' we can use the `case_when()` and `mutate()` function in `dplyr`. The combination of these two functions allows us to create a new column that will label a row based on a certain logical criteria (*i.e.* if p-value is less than 0.05, label as "X").

A `case_when()` statement has the following syntax:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#sample code
mutate(col_name = case_when(
  LOGICAL_STATEMENT_A ~ "label_if_statement_A_is_TRUE",
  LOGICAL_STATEMENT_B ~ "label_if_statement_B_is_TRUE",
  TRUE ~ "label to give if none of the conditions above are TRUE"
))
```

<br></br>

**Note** that the label will be given based on the condition that is met **first** (top-to-bottom order!). As an example, let's label the rows in `dat` based on their Log2FC and padj values. We want to label genes as "UP" or "DOWN" based on if they satisfy both the padj and log2FoldChange conditions. We can used the `&` operator which means AND to only label a gene if condition1 AND condition2 are true.

```{r}
labelled_dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(up_down = case_when(
    padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange > 1 ~ "UP", # label genes in the top right quadrant of the volcano plot
    padj < 0.05 & log2FoldChange < -1 ~ "DOWN", # label genes in the top left quadrant of the volcano plot
    TRUE ~ "NONE"
  ))
```

<br></br>

Now we can plot this!

```{r}
# NOTE how we are coloring the point in the plot based on the up_down column we just created above!!
labelled_dat %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = up_down)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed")

```

<br></br>

That looks better! Of course we can make this prettier, you should explore this by yourselves, but here's an example!

<br></br>

```{r echo = FALSE}
labelled_dat %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = up_down)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", colour = "black"),
    legend.title = element_blank(), 
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black", size = 12),
    panel.border = element_rect(linewidth = 2)
  ) +
  labs(x = "Log2FoldChange", y = "-Log10(Adjusted P-Value)")
```

<br></br>

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**One thought:** You could also colour a defined set of points (genes in a volcano plot) to show how/if those points were upregulated/downregulated with reference to all other points. This can be useful if you already have genes of interest in mind (*i.e.* amino acid transporters or glycolysis genes) that you want to visualize in reference to all other points.

To show an **example**, I will select the top 10 genes with the highest padj values and I will annotate them in the volcano plot. Follow the example below:

To achieve this we will perform **3 steps**:

1.  Create a character vector containing the genes of interest. In this case, suppose I am interested in the top 10 genes with the lowest p-values.
2.  Next, using a `case_when()` function we label the genes of interest.
3.  Finally, we plot a volcano plot, but only colouring the genes of interest.

**Keep in mind that** you can also manually make a character vector of genes of interest if you have specific genes that you're interested in!

First, create a character vector containing the `gene_id` of the top 10 genes with the lowest p-values. We do this by arranging the dataframe by adjusted p-value, only take the top 10 genes, select the `gene_id` column, and convert the dataframe to a vector with `pull()`.

```{r}
topGenes <- dat %>%
  arrange(padj) %>%
  head(n = 10) %>%
  dplyr::select(gene_id) %>%
  pull()
```

<br></br>

Next, use `mutate()` and `case_when()` to add a label to the selected `gene_ids`. The `%in%` operator symbolizes if a value is IN a vector.

```{r}
dat_annotated <- dat %>%
  mutate(annotation  = case_when(
    gene_id %in% topGenes ~ "GOI",
    TRUE ~ "normal"
  ))
```

<br></br>

Finally, plot the volcano plot - keeping sure to only highlight the genes of interest. We can also change the default colours of the points using `scale_colour_manual`!

```{r}
#BiocManager::install("ggrepel")
library(ggrepel) #allows for the geom_text_repel argument, places labels strategically to not overlap 

dat_annotated %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = annotation)) + 
  geom_point() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = c(-1, 1), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_text_repel(data = filter(dat_annotated, annotation == "GOI"),
                  aes(label = gene_id),
                  colour = "black",
                  size = 3,
                  max.overlaps = Inf,
                  min.segment.length = 0) +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("red", "grey")) 
```

<br></br>

Cool! We can now see where the genes with the lowest padj values are located! Imagine if you had a list of 100 genes in a metabolic pathway that you wanted to quickly visualize in your DE data, the plot above could have been really useful!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 2. Bar Plots

The volcano plot provides a good starting birds-eye view of our data. But what if we wanted to visualize a more focused version of the data? Perhaps we want to show how many genes are up/downregulated at different log2FoldChanges? One way to achieve this is using bar plots. Let's try this out!

First, we will create a new column to group our genes based on their log2FoldChange. Using `mutate()`, we will calculate the absolute value of the log2FoldChange and use an `if_else()` function (a handy, short version of an if statement) to label genes as up or downregulated. `if_else()` syntax is as follows: `if_else(LOGICAL_STATMENT, "CASE IF TRUE", "CASE IF FALSE":)`. We'll also once again use `case_when()` to label our data based roughly on the magnitude of the fold change.

```{r}
labelled_dat2 <- dat %>%
  mutate(abs_l2fc = abs(log2FoldChange), # take absolute value of fold change
         up_down = if_else(log2FoldChange <= 0, "DOWN", "UP") # label genes as up or downregulated
         ) %>% 
  mutate(l2fc = case_when( # bin our genes based on fold change
    abs_l2fc >=4 ~ ">4",
    abs_l2fc >=3 ~ "3",
    abs_l2fc >=2 ~ "2",
    abs_l2fc >=1 ~ "1",
    TRUE ~ "<1"
  ))

labelled_dat2
```

<br></br>

Now let's plot a bar graph with our labeled data. Note that below we will use `fill` to colour our bars. When making bar plots and some other geoms, `fill` specifies the inside fill colour and `colour` specifies the outside line colour. You should explore the difference between `geom_bar()` and `geom_col()`.

```{r}
labelled_dat2 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x=l2fc, fill = up_down)) +
  geom_bar(color="black") +
  theme_classic()
```

<br></br>

This is a good start, but it seems like our x-axis is out of order. We can fix this using factors. Remember that factors are a way to organize categorical data in R. Lets organize our `l2fc` column such that the labels go from lowest to highest l2fc

```{r}
# First, transform the l2fc column into a factor with factor()
labelled_dat2$l2fc <- factor(labelled_dat2$l2fc)

# Let's check the order of the factors in l2fc
levels(labelled_dat2$l2fc)
```

<br></br>

That isn't the desired order! We want it to go in numerical order. Lets change it:

```{r}
# NOTE that we need to input the same number of labels and with their same name!!
labelled_dat2$l2fc <- factor(labelled_dat2$l2fc, levels = c("<1","1","2","3",">4"))

# Print the levels again to see if they changed
levels(labelled_dat2$l2fc)
```

Great! Now let's plot again.

```{r}
ggplot(labelled_dat2, aes(x=l2fc, fill = up_down)) +
  geom_bar(color="black") +
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "Log2(FC)", y = "# of Genes", fill = "Regulated") # modify the labels!
```

<br></br>

Okay, the plot is now in the order that we want. This plot might not be suitable for your main figures, but could act as a supplementary figure and can help you in your exploratory analysis!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Visualizing the Top 10 Highest and Lowest Up/Downregulated Genes

We were able to visualize our samples using PCA plots and the overall distribution of our DE genes using volcano plots. Let's now zoom into our data and plot the `log2FoldChange` of a subset of genes that were up/downregulated.

First, let's create new dataframe objects to store the top 10 most upregulated and downregulated genes.

```{r}
# Top 10 upregulated genes
top10Genes <- dat %>%
  arrange(desc(log2FoldChange)) %>% 
  head(n = 10)

top10Genes

# Top 10 downregulated genes
bot10Genes <- dat %>%
  arrange(log2FoldChange) %>% 
  head(n = 10)

bot10Genes
```

<br></br>

To start, let's plot the top 10 most upregulated genes using a bar plot.

```{r}
top10Genes %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_col()
```

<br></br>

This looks **BAD** - the bars are not organized as in descending order and the x-axis text overlap with each other making them impossible to read. Let's try to fix this.

First, let's reorganize the bars from highest to lowest. You could do this be refactoring, but we can accomplish this today with `scale_x_discrete(limits = )`.

```{r}
# Take the 'gene_id' column in order and store it as a character vector
order <- top10Genes %>% 
  dplyr::select(gene_id) %>% 
  pull()

# Plot again but arrange the bars based on the order of the character vector
top10Genes %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = order) # use the scale_x_discrete() function with the limits= argument to order the plot
```

<br></br>

We ordered that bars as desired, but it is still hard to read the x-axis values.

To make the x-axis more readable we could either **1)** rotate the x-axis values or **2)** make a horizontal bar plot.

1)  Rotate the x-axis values with `theme()`

```{r}
top10Genes %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = order) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, vjust = 0.5, hjust=1))

```

<br></br>

2)  Make a horizontal bar plot with `coord_flip()`

```{r}
top10Genes %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = order) +
  coord_flip()
```

<br></br>

We can now finally read the values in our plot! Note that the order of the bar plot was 'reversed' when we used `coord_flip()`. How could you solved this problem?

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Next, let's add error bars to our plot. Error bars are useful to visualize how confident we are that the log2FC values plotted are "real" (it can tell use how tightly grouped our replicates were).

DESeq2 calculates the standard error for the `log2FoldChange` called `lfcSE`. We can use this value to create error bars using the ggplot2 `geom_errobar()` function. For this function we need to input the limits for the error bars using `ymin =` and `ymax =` arguments. Note that this is performed in another call to `aesthetics` - this is necessary because `ymin` and `ymax` will vary *depending* on our data.

```{r}
top10Genes %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin= log2FoldChange - lfcSE, ymax = log2FoldChange + lfcSE), width = 0.4) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = order) +
  coord_flip()
```

<br></br>

Also note the order of the `geom` calls. What happens if you reverse the order of `geom_errorbar()` and `geom_col()`?

You could replicate the above plot for downregulated genes! Regardless, it's often useful to show both upregulated and downregulated genes in the same plot? Let's try plotting the top 10 upregulated and downregulated genes together. To do this we will make a new dataframe that contains the top 10 up and downregulated genes and then plot it like usual.

Make our joined dataframe using `bind_rows()`. This function slaps two dataframes together rowwise.

```{r}
# Bind our two top 10 genes dataframes using the bind_rows() column
joined_top10 <- bind_rows(top10Genes, bot10Genes) %>%
  mutate(up_down = if_else(log2FoldChange > 0, "UP", "DOWN")) %>%
  arrange(log2FoldChange)

# To organize our bar plot, we can also extract the order of our organized genes
order_joined <- joined_top10 %>% 
  dplyr::select(gene_id) %>% 
  pull()
```

<br></br>

Now let's plot our data (I also added some extra code to make the plot prettier - I encourage you to play around with the code and find ways to make your plot more appealing!). Try Googling parts of the code that you don't understand, learn more about them and add them to your 'plotting repertoire'.

```{r}
joined_top10 %>% 
  ggplot(aes(x = gene_id, y = log2FoldChange, fill = up_down)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin= log2FoldChange - lfcSE, ymax =log2FoldChange + lfcSE), width = 0.4) +
  geom_col(color = "black", width = 0.8) +
  scale_x_discrete(limits = order_joined) +
  coord_flip()+ 
  labs(y = "log2(FC)", x= "Gene ID", fill = "Regulation") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  theme_light() +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(-17,17), breaks = seq(-15, 15, 5), expand = c(0,0)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("red", "forestgreen")) +
  theme(
    panel.border = element_rect(color = "black"),
    panel.grid = element_line(colour = "white"),
    axis.text = element_text(colour = "black"))
```

<br></br>

**NOTE** that you can make this same plot with any amount of genes you wanted to show. You could have also plotted some genes of interest!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Extracting and Plotting Normalized Counts

**Why would we want to visualize counts instead of fold change?** Think about the following, gene A and gene B might both have a fold-change of 4. Gene A changed from 1 mapped read to 4 mapped reads, whereas gene B changed from 200 mapped reads to 800 mapped reads. Which one do you feel is ***actually*** differentially expressed?

To plot normalized counts, we will first extract the DESeq2 normalized counts from the `dds` object and put them into a dataframe.

```{r}
# Extract the normalized counts and prepare the data for plotting
norm_dds <- estimateSizeFactors(dds)
normalized_counts <- counts(norm_dds, normalized = TRUE) %>% 
  as.data.frame() %>%
  rownames_to_column(var = "gene_id") %>% # convert the rownames to a column
  pivot_longer(!gene_id, names_to = "Sample", values_to = "count") %>% # converts data to a "tidy" format for plotting. Check the documentation for this handy function
  separate(Sample, into = c("Sample", "replicate"), sep = "_rep") %>% # splits a column into multiple columns based on a separator
  dplyr::select(-replicate) %>% # drop a column
  mutate(Sample = factor(Sample)) # convert column to a factor

# Change the order of the levels
levelsOrder <- c("chlamy_1h", "chlamy_12h")
normalized_counts$Sample <- factor(normalized_counts$Sample, levels = levelsOrder)

# Visualize the dataframe
normalized_counts
```

<br></br>

Now let's plot the normalized counts for random gene:

```{r}
# pull the gene_id of row 123 from our original data
gene_of_interest <- pull(dat[123, 1]) 

# Let's select all rows in our 'normalized_counts' dataframe that have the same 'gene_id' as our `gene_of_interest`
normalized_counts %>%
  filter(gene_id == gene_of_interest) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Sample, y = count, color = Sample)) + 
    geom_jitter(width = 0.2, size = 3) +
    theme_classic()

```

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Plotting a Z-Score Heatmap

**What are Z-scores?** The amount by which a gene deviates (Standard deviations) in a specific sample from the gene’s average across all samples. That means, how many standard deviations is my value away from the mean of a row (gene). You can read more about it [here](https://www.simplypsychology.org/z-score.html)

Let's calculate the Z-score values for our normalized count data.

We need to prepare our data first. Similar to `rlog()`, `vst()` normalizes and transforms our count data in a manner that stablizes the variance. `assay()` simply pulls out the count values as a dataframe. The result will be a dataframe where rownames are genes and columns are samples.

```{r}
vsd <- assay(vst(dds))
```

`scale()` will calculate the Z-scores for each gene and store them as a matrix. `t()` is a function that *transposes* the data (i.e. the columns turn into the rows and the rows columns). We need to perform this step solely due to the way `scale()` accepts its input data, but we undo our transposition with a second `t()` call.

```{r}
Z <- t(scale(t(vsd)))

# Check the Z-score matrix
head(Z)
```

<br></br>

First, let's plot our entire data set - this will take a while!

```{r}
# Remove rows with NA values - if not we will get errors!
Z_no_NA <- na.omit(Z)

# Now lets plot using pheatmap() 
pheatmap(Z_no_NA, 
         main = "Z-Score Heatmap")
```

<br></br>

Nice, but this heatmap is hardly informative. Let's narrow down the scope and solely investigate genes with the highest variation in a row.

Let's extract the top 20 genes with the highest row variation in our data! `rowVar()` calculates the genes with the highest variation across all samples. `order()` orders the data in decreasing fashion.

```{r}
# Extract the row indices (akak the location in the matrix) of the rows with the highest variation
topVarGenes <- rowVars(vsd) %>% 
  order(decreasing = TRUE) %>% 
  head(20) 

# Subset the Z-score matrix for only the row we're interested in (stored in topVarGenes)
Z_topGenes <- Z[topVarGenes,] 
```

<br></br>

Now lets plots again using `pheatmap()`

```{r}
pheatmap(Z_topGenes,
         main = "Top 20 Genes")
```

<br></br>

Interesting! We can definitely see two distinct clusters. Perhaps it would be interesting to explore those genes! Z-score heatmaps are a good way to do some exploratory analysis. There are also many ways you can modify your pheatmap aesthetically. I encourage you to go and modify your heatmap from the default!

------------------------------------------------------------------------

<br></br>

# Conclusions

There are multiple ways to visualize RNA-seq data. Ask yourself some questions when plotting:

1.  What am I trying to convey with my plot?
2.  In what ways has this data been visualized in other papers?
3.  Is my plot exploratory or targeted?
4.  What conclusions can I make from my plot?

Explore many different options and practice, practice, practice!
